meta.title: Who really said "A good speech should be like a woman's skirt"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Churchill used the joke, but did not invent it — it was an anonymous American newspaper gag by 1920, twenty-two years before the first Churchill attribution, and it started out about a bathing suit.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'A good speech should be like a woman's skirt'?
meta.ogDescription: An anonymous 1920 American newspaper joke. A congressman used the speech version in October 1920; the first Churchill attribution is 1942.

answer.label: Not original to Churchill — an anonymous 1920 joke
answer.authorDates: Anonymous American newspaper joke · in circulation by 1920
answer.sourceLine: Churchill did use the gag — he is reported saying a version of it in 1942 — but he did not invent it. It was already an anonymous American newspaper joke by 1920, twenty-two years earlier, and it began life as a joke about a bathing suit and a manuscript. The earliest known version applied to a speech comes from an Indiana congressman in October 1920.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: 1918 — a manuscript and a bathing suit

source.excerpt: A speech should be very much like a woman's skirt—long enough to cover the subject but short enough to be interesting.
trail: The joke evolves out of an older ‘length’ gag. In 1918 the ideal manuscript is compared to an up-to-date lady’s bathing suit: ‘short enough to be interesting and long enough to cover the subject’ the full chain ↗.
By May 1920 a Buffalo newspaperman applies the skirt version to a newspaper column — and prints it in quotation marks, which signals a saying already in circulation rather than one he coined.

The version above, applied to a speech, was used by Indiana congressman Richard N. Elliott in October 1920. The earliest Churchill attribution appears in a New York column in 1942, twenty-two years later, in the ‘lady’s dress’ form.
source.excerptNote: The earliest known form applied to a speech. Elliott did not present it as his own invention either — by late 1920 this was simply a joke going round, which is exactly the condition in which quotations lose their authors and later acquire famous ones.
source.rightsNote: Free to reuse. The originating texts are anonymous American newspaper material from 1918–1920, published well before 1930 and therefore in the public domain in the United States; you may reproduce the 1920 wording in full. Because the joke is not Churchill’s, his estate’s copyright to 2035 is irrelevant to it. The one thing to avoid is quoting the 1942 columnist’s reported Churchill phrasing as though it were a verified Churchill utterance — that is a journalist’s paraphrase, and it is his text, not Churchill’s. This is not legal advice.

author.name: Winston Churchill
author.heading: Why it gets pinned on Churchill
author.metaLine: 1874–1965 · British statesman, historian and Nobel laureate in Literature
author.bio: Sir Winston Churchill is the great attractor of orphaned witticisms: any remark about oratory, brevity or wit drifts toward him eventually. In this case the drift had real help, because he genuinely did use the joke — which makes it a subtler problem than a pure fabrication. Using a joke and originating one are different things, and quotation sites almost never distinguish them.

misattribution.heading: The attribution problem
misattribution.intro: A more interesting case than the usual fake, because the credit is not simply wrong. Churchill really did say a version of it — he just said it two decades after everyone else.

items.who: Used by Churchill, not coined by him
items.why: The first Churchill attribution is 1942, in a New York column reporting him. The joke is documented from 1918–1920, so he was repeating a stock gag that was older than his premiership the chain ↗.

items.who: A manuscript, then a newspaper column
items.why: The 1918 precursor is about a manuscript compared to a bathing suit; by May 1920 it is a newspaper column compared to a skirt; only in October 1920 does it settle on a speech.

Skirt or dress or bathing suit; ‘create interest’ or ‘be interesting’ or ‘be attractive’; applied to a speech, a sermon, a letter or a column. There is no canonical form because there was no original author.
The theologian Ronald Knox is sometimes named as the source. No evidence supports it.

misattribution.truthLine: An anonymous American newspaper joke in circulation by 1920 — used by a congressman that October, and not attributed to Churchill until 1942 the evidence ↗.

context.heading: Why it resonates
lead: It survives because it is genuinely useful advice about speaking, smuggled inside a joke — cover the material, then stop. Advice that arrives as a laugh gets repeated far longer than advice that arrives as a rule.

It has also aged unevenly. The gag depends on a 1920s frisson about hemlines that has largely evaporated, leaving a line that lands today more as a period piece than as wit — which may be why it now travels chiefly as a Churchill anecdote rather than on its own merits.
detailsBody: 1918: a manuscript should be like an up-to-date lady’s bathing suit — short enough to be interesting, long enough to cover the subject.
May 1920: a newspaper column compared to a woman’s skirt — printed in quotation marks, i.e. already circulating.
October 1920: Rep. Richard N. Elliott applies it to a speech — the earliest known speech version.
1942: a New York columnist reports Churchill using the ‘lady’s dress’ form — the first Churchill attribution.
The gap between the joke and the famous name: twenty-two years.
context.pull: He really did say it. He just said it twenty-two years after everyone else.
